title: Purpose of the Offset Geometry
learningObjectives: Explain why an offset hanger is used in a process plant.
student: Why is an offset hanger used instead of suspending the equipment directly below the overhead beam?
instructor: The offset geometry provides clearance from nearby piping, vessels, access space, and structural members while still transferring the suspended load to the overhead support.

title: External Load Application
learningObjectives: Identify where the external load enters the hanger.
student: Where does the principal external load enter the hanger, and how should it be idealized?
instructor: The suspended component applies a downward concentrated load P through the chain at attachment point E.

title: Overhead Support Condition
learningObjectives: Describe the fixed-support idealization at D.
student: How should the overhead connection at D be idealized in the simplified mechanics model?
instructor: Idealize D as a fixed support that prevents horizontal translation, vertical translation, and rotation. It can therefore supply two reaction-force components and a reaction moment.

title: Dominant Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace the suspended load to the building structure.
student: Trace the dominant load path from the suspended component to the overhead structural beam.
instructor: Suspended component → chain → attachment E → curved hanger → fixed connection D → overhead structural beam.

title: Selection of Section a-a
learningObjectives: Explain why the designated section carries substantial bending demand.
student: Why is section a-a a reasonable location for the assigned strength check?
instructor: Section a-a lies in the main load path and carries the bending moment produced by the horizontal offset between the vertical load line at E and the section.

title: Governing Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Recognize flexural normal stress as the assigned criterion.
student: What mechanical response is expected to govern the base problem?
instructor: The assigned criterion is maximum elastic normal stress from bending at section a-a. Internal shear is present, but shear stress is not the governing check specified for this exercise.

title: Parameters Governing Capacity
learningObjectives: Relate allowable load to material, offset, and section properties.
student: Which variables most directly control the maximum allowable suspended load?
instructor: The allowable bending stress, horizontal offset L, and section modulus govern capacity directly. The section modulus depends on the centroid, second moment of area, and governing extreme-fiber distance established by B, H, t1, and t2.

title: Student-Generated Hanger Idealization
learningObjectives: Translate the hanger assembly into a mechanics model.
gradingNotes: Students should attempt the structural idealization before consulting the instructor reference figure.
commonMistakes: Common omissions are the fixed-end moment, the perpendicular offset L, the critical cut, or an explicit definition of the three nonoverlapping section rectangles.
student: Before using the instructor reference figure, replace the real hanger with a simplified mechanics model. Show fixed support D, downward load P at E, section a-a, horizontal offset L, and the assigned three-rectangle cross-section.
instructor: A valid model shows the hanger fixed at D, a downward point load P at E, a vertical cut at section a-a, and perpendicular horizontal distance L from the load line to the cut. The section consists of a B by t2 top flange, a t1 by (H - 2t2) web, and a (t1 + 2t2) by t2 bottom flange.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the allowable-stress model.
student: State the assumptions used to convert the real hanger into the simplified model.
instructor: Assume static loading, a concentrated vertical load, a fixed support at D, linear-elastic material response, small deformation, and standard straight-beam flexure at section a-a. Neglect hanger self-weight, chain dynamics, local connection behavior, fatigue, impact, out-of-plane effects, contact, stress concentrations, and curved-beam corrections.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Sequence equilibrium, composite-section, and allowable-load calculations.
student: List the mechanics calculation sequence required to determine the allowable load.
instructor: Determine the internal shear and moment at section a-a; divide the section into three nonoverlapping rectangles; calculate total area and centroid; apply the parallel-axis theorem to obtain the centroidal second moment of area; calculate both extreme-fiber distances; use the larger stress magnitude to define the governing section modulus; set the governing bending stress equal to the allowable stress; and solve for Pmax.

title: Boundary Condition and Reactions at D
learningObjectives: Identify all reaction resultants admitted at D.
student: State the boundary condition at D and list the reaction resultants it can supply.
instructor: D is fixed and can supply horizontal reaction Dx, vertical reaction Dy, and reaction moment MD. Under the assigned vertical loading, Dy and MD are nonzero.

title: Internal Shear and Bending Moment
learningObjectives: Use section equilibrium to determine resultants in terms of the unknown load.
commonMistakes: The bend radius R does not replace the perpendicular moment arm L. Use the horizontal distance from the vertical load line to section a-a.
student: Cut the hanger at section a-a and determine the internal shear force and bending moment in terms of P and L.
instructor: The internal shear magnitude is |V| = P, and the bending-moment magnitude is |M| = PL. At the allowable load, |V| = {{hanger_V_N}} N and |M| = {{hanger_M_Nmm}} N·mm.

title: Composite Areas and Centroid Locations
learningObjectives: Define nonoverlapping component areas and their centroid coordinates.
student: Using the bottom of the section as the reference, calculate the area and centroid coordinate of each nonoverlapping rectangle and the total area.
instructor: Bottom flange: Ab = (t1 + 2t2)t2 = {{hanger_A_bottom_mm2}} mm2, with yb = t2/2. Web: Aw = t1(H - 2t2) = {{hanger_A_web_mm2}} mm2, with yw = H/2. Top flange: At = Bt2 = {{hanger_A_top_mm2}} mm2, with yt = H - t2/2. Total area = {{hanger_A_total_mm2}} mm2.

title: Centroid of the Unsymmetric Section
learningObjectives: Locate the neutral axis using the composite-area relation.
commonMistakes: The section is not symmetric about its horizontal mid-depth because the top and bottom flange widths differ.
student: Determine the centroid coordinate measured upward from the bottom of section a-a.
instructor: Using ȳ = ΣAiyi/ΣAi, the centroid is {{hanger_ybar_mm}} mm above the bottom surface.

title: Centroidal Second Moment of Area
learningObjectives: Apply the parallel-axis theorem to an unsymmetric section.
commonMistakes: Use each rectangle's own centroidal inertia and add Aidi2. Do not overlap the web and flanges.
student: Determine the centroidal second moment of area of section a-a about the horizontal neutral axis.
instructor: Apply I = Σ[Ic,i + Ai(yi - ȳ)2] to the bottom flange, web, and top flange. The result is {{hanger_I_mm4}} mm4.

title: Extreme-Fiber Distances and Governing Fiber
learningObjectives: Compare top and bottom extreme-fiber distances.
student: Calculate the distances from the neutral axis to the top and bottom surfaces. Which extreme fiber governs the allowable-stress calculation?
instructor: ctop = H - ȳ = {{hanger_c_top_mm}} mm, and cbottom = ȳ = {{hanger_c_bottom_mm}} mm. Therefore ccrit = {{hanger_c_crit_mm}} mm, and the {{hanger_governing_fiber}} governs.

title: Governing Section Modulus
learningObjectives: Calculate the section modulus associated with the governing fiber.
student: Determine the governing elastic section modulus for the allowable-load calculation.
instructor: Scrit = I/ccrit = {{hanger_S_mm3}} mm3.

title: Maximum Allowable Suspended Load
learningObjectives: Solve the flexure criterion for the maximum load.
commonMistakes: Because 1 MPa = 1 N/mm2, retain N and mm consistently. Use the governing extreme-fiber distance, not H/2.
student: Use the allowable bending stress to determine the maximum allowable suspended load. Then calculate the top- and bottom-fiber stresses at that load.
instructor: Set σallow = PmaxLccrit/I. Thus Pmax = σallowI/(Lccrit) = {{hanger_Pmax_N}} N = {{hanger_Pmax_kN}} kN. At this load, the top-fiber stress magnitude is {{hanger_sigma_top_MPa}} MPa and the bottom-fiber stress magnitude is {{hanger_sigma_bottom_MPa}} MPa.

title: Stress Sense and Geometry Sensitivity
learningObjectives: Interpret stress sense and compare capacity improvements.
student: For the downward load shown, identify the extreme fibers in tension and compression. Then explain how increasing section depth, moving material away from the neutral axis, or reducing L affects allowable load.
instructor: For the shown load and fixed support to the right, the {{hanger_tension_fiber}} is in tension and the {{hanger_compression_fiber}} is in compression. Increasing section depth or moving material away from the neutral axis increases I and section modulus, often strongly. Reducing L increases allowable load inversely because the moment is PL.

title: Engineering Assessment and Model Limits
learningObjectives: State a bounded allowable-load recommendation and omitted checks.
student: State the allowable suspended load and recommend one mechanics-based modification if more capacity is required. Identify important checks omitted from the base analysis.
instructor:
{{hanger_assessment}}

A complete design must also evaluate local connection and weld stresses, chain and attachment capacity, curved-beam effects, out-of-plane loading, stress concentrations, fatigue, impact and dynamics, deflection, manufacturing tolerances, inspection requirements, and applicable lifting-support standards.
